One Another
WUN uh-NUTH-ur
noun phrase (church life)
Rendering Greek allelon, of one another, the reciprocal pronoun marking the mutual duties of the members of Christ's body.

📖 Biblical Definition

The "one anothers" are the reciprocal commands of the New Testament — love one another, forbear one another, exhort one another, serve one another, prefer one another — that describe the mutual life of the body of Christ. The word is allelon, recurring scores of times. Paul gathers many in one place: "Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another... distributing to the necessity of saints" (Rom 12:10,13), and earlier, "we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another" (Rom 12:5). To the Ephesians he writes, "Forbearing one another in love; Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Eph 4:2–3), and to the Thessalonians, "comfort yourselves together, and edify one another" (1 Thess 5:11). These mutual duties are the warm and ordinary fabric of congregational life. Yet they do not level the offices Christ has set: the same Paul who commands mutual submission also commands wives to submit to husbands and the flock to obey their elders. The body has many members of differing function, "not... the same office" (Rom 12:4). This dictionary confesses the one anothers as the genuine reciprocity of love within the church, lived out under, not against, the order of headship and office that God has appointed.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The reciprocal commands of the New Testament — to love, forbear, exhort, serve, and prefer one another — describing the mutual life of Christ's body. They are real reciprocity in love, yet do not abolish the differing offices God has set.

ONE ANOTHER, noun phrase. The reciprocal duties of the members of Christ's body.

Rendering the Greek allelon, gathered richly in Romans 12, Ephesians 4, and the Thessalonian letters.

"Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another" (Rom 12:10).

It requires the mutual love, forbearance, exhortation, and service of all the saints.

It does not level the offices of the church but is lived under the order God has set.

📖 Key Scripture

Rom 12:10 — "Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;"

Eph 4:2 — "With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love;"

1 Thess 5:11 — "Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do."

Rom 12:5 — "So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The one anothers are abused where "mutuality" is made to abolish office and headship, as though reciprocal love and ordained authority could not stand together in the same body.

expand to see more

A levelling reading seizes the one anothers — especially "submitting yourselves one to another" (Eph 5:21) — to argue that Scripture knows no fixed office, no male eldership, no headship in the home, only undifferentiated equals. But the very passages that command mutual duty also command particular order: the same context that says "submitting yourselves one to another" goes on to direct wives, children, and servants specifically (Eph 5:22ff). Paul's image is a body of many members with differing functions, "not... the same office" (Rom 12:4). Reciprocal love does not dissolve appointed authority; it adorns it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is that the church is a true family, not a mere institution: its members are "members one of another" (Rom 12:5), bound to love, forbear, comfort, and edify in a hundred ordinary acts. The recovery of the one anothers cures both a cold, transactional churchmanship and a flattening egalitarianism — for warm mutual love and ordained office are not rivals but companions in the one body.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase renders the single Greek reciprocal pronoun allelon, of one another, which threads the apostolic letters.

expand to see more

Greek allelon, the reciprocal pronoun, recurs roughly fifty times across the New Testament.

It governs verbs of love, forbearance, exhortation, service, and honour among the saints.

Romans 12, Ephesians 4, and 1 Thessalonians gather many of these duties in close compass.

The body image (Rom 12:4–5) frames mutuality without erasing differing function.

English one another simply distributes the reciprocity across the members of the body.

Usage

"The church practised the one anothers, bearing one another's burdens without erasing the elders' office."

"He showed how the one another commands warm a congregation without levelling the order God set."

"To love one another is no rival to honouring those over you in the Lord; both are commanded."
